WHAT01/50

MEAI 502 · CS 4082 · Spring 2026

Introduction to
Machine Learning

Lecture 1 — What machine learning is, and why now

Dr Naila Marir · Effat University · College of Engineering

Speaker notes

Don't open with logistics. Open with a question: “How many of you used something powered by machine learning before you got to this room today?” Unlocking a phone with a face, a maps route, a spam filter, an autocomplete. Nearly every hand goes up.

Then: “How many of you could explain what it was doing?” Far fewer. “That gap is this course.”

Housekeeping can wait until the end — the syllabus walk-through is its own session.
WHAT02/50

“AI is the new electricity.”

Andrew Ng · Stanford University

A hundred years ago, electricity transformed every major industry in turn — transport, manufacturing, agriculture, healthcare. Machine learning is doing that now.

Speaker notes

Open the lecture here, not on the syllabus. Say the quote, then stop talking for a beat and let it sit.

Unpack the analogy, because it does real work. Electricity was not one product — it was a general-purpose technology. Nobody sells “electricity solutions”; it simply became part of how everything else is built. Ng's claim is that machine learning is the same kind of thing: not one industry, but an input to all of them.

Make it concrete and local: ask the room to name an industry in Saudi Arabia and work out together where ML already sits in it. Aramco predictive maintenance, bank fraud detection, Absher, hospital triage, retail demand forecasting, Vision 2030 smart-city projects. They will find one in seconds.

Be honest about the limits of the analogy if a sharp student pushes: electricity is a commodity with one well-understood behaviour; ML systems fail in ways electricity does not — they inherit bias from data, they degrade as the world changes, and they can be confidently wrong. That tension is a thread you pull all semester.

Attribution: Ng has used this line since roughly 2016–2017, in talks and interviews rather than in one canonical paper. Say “Andrew Ng” and move on.

WHAT06/50

01

What is machine learning?

  • Three systems you use every day
  • The classical definition
  • Why programming isn't enough

Speaker notes

WHAT07/50

You use it many times a day

You probably used several of these before you walked into this room today — and not one of them was built by someone writing down the rules.

Speaker notes

Work the room. Ask them to raise a hand for each one they used today — search, photos, a recommendation, voice, spam, face unlock. Hands stay up. “That is six times before breakfast.”

Take the examples one at a time and keep them concrete, the way Ng does: “How do I make a sushi roll?” → search. Tagging friends in a photo. Finishing a Star Wars film and being offered the next thing. Dictating a message. The “you've won a million dollars” email that never reaches you. Unlocking the phone with your face.

The spam filter is the strongest teaching case, so dwell there: the problem fights back. Spammers change their behaviour deliberately, so a fixed set of rules decays within weeks. A learning system retrains. Keep that image — you return to it when you cover distribution shift.

Bring it local so it is theirs, not Silicon Valley's: Absher, STC support bots, Careem matching, Saudi bank fraud alerts, Jahez recommendations.
WHAT08/50

And it is moving into industry

Beyond the apps on your phone, machine learning is moving into energy, healthcare and factories — the places where being right actually matters.

Speaker notes

Ng's three industrial examples, and the pivot from “convenient” to “consequential”.

Say the stakes out loud, because it reframes the whole course: “If a music recommendation is wrong, you skip the song. If a diagnosis is wrong, someone is harmed.” That is why evaluation gets its own week, and why we keep returning to how you know a model is any good.

Localise all three — Saudi Arabia has real versions of each: NEOM and the Vision 2030 renewables programme, hospital imaging at KFSH, and Aramco predictive maintenance on industrial equipment.

This is also a good moment to plant project ambition: “Your semester project can be in any of these areas.”
WHAT09/50

“Machine learning is the field of study that gives computers the ability to learn without being explicitly programmed.”

Arthur Samuel · 1959

Speaker notes

Original slides 8–9 (the French duplicate is removed).

Be honest about provenance: this is the wording universally attributed to Samuel, but it does not appear verbatim in his 1959 paper — it's a paraphrase that stuck. Say “attributed to” if a sharp student pushes. What Samuel did do is more impressive than the quote: he wrote a checkers program that improved by playing against itself, and it eventually beat him.

Land the key phrase: “without being explicitly programmed” — everything today hangs on it.
WHAT10/50

Programming vs learning

Traditional programming

Input:   x=0, y=1, z=2

program {
  f(x,y,z) = x + 3·y·z
  return f(x,y,z)
}

Output:  6
vs

Machine learning

Input:   a photograph

program {
  f(picture) = ???
}

Output:  “flower”

You can write the arithmetic rule in one line. Nobody can write the flower rule. So instead of writing f, we give the machine thousands of labelled pictures and let it find f itself.

Speaker notes

Original slides 10–11 — the pivotal slide of the first half. Don't rush it.

Push them: “Define a flower in pixels. Go on — try.” They'll offer petals, colour, symmetry. Counter each: a white flower, a wilted flower, a photograph taken from above, a flower in shadow, a plastic flower. Every rule they propose breaks on a case you can name in five seconds.

Then the reframe: “The rule exists — you just can't articulate it. Learning is how we recover a rule we cannot state.” That sentence is the whole course in one line.
WHY NOW11/50

02

Why now?

  • The four enablers
  • Where the applications are
  • How it started

Speaker notes

WHY NOW12/50

Four things changed

1

Data

Web, sensors, medical records, transactions. The raw material of learning became abundant and cheap to store.

2

Compute

GPUs and TPUs. Hardware built to render triangles turned out to be exactly right for matrix multiplication.

3

Algorithms

Backpropagation, ReLU, dropout, batch norm, Adam, attention. Scale alone would not have been enough.

4

Software

scikit-learn, PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX. One lab session now does what took a PhD student a year in 2010.

The core ideas are decades old. Data, compute, algorithms and software are what finally made them work.

Speaker notes

Original slide 13, expanded — the source deck listed three enablers; algorithms belong in the list. Attention (2017) is not a scaling result, it's an algorithmic one, and without ReLU and better optimizers the deep networks of 2012 would not have trained at all.

Make the hardware point vivid: the GPU exists because of video games. Nobody designed it for this.

Point at enabler 4 and tell them it's personal: “You will do in Lab 1, in one session, what was a research contribution fifteen years ago.”
WHY NOW13/50

Where it pays off

Add a fourth category the original list predates: generative systems that produce text, images, code and audio rather than only classifying it.

Speaker notes

Original slide 13's application list, preserved and then extended.

Category 3 is worth dwelling on: it's not one program with settings — it's a program that builds a different model for each user. That's a genuinely different way to think about software.

The fourth category is the bridge to section 08. Don't unpack it yet; just plant it.
WHY NOW14/50

Seventy years in one picture

The field is older than it looks. Almost every idea below predates the students in this room — what changed recently is scale, not invention.

Speaker notes

Original slide 15's timeline figure, given its own slide so it can be read.

Walk left to right, but do not narrate every box. Land three points: Turing at the far left (1930s–50s), backpropagation in the middle (1986), and the deep learning explosion at the right (2010s).

Ask them to find the gap — there's a visible thinning between roughly 1970 and 1985. That's the first AI winter: funding collapsed, and the field nearly died. Progress was not monotonic.
WHY NOW15/50

The milestones that matter

  • 1950

    The Turing Test

    Turing asks whether machines can think — and reframes it as a question about behaviour.

  • 1952

    Samuel's checkers player

    A program that improved by playing itself. Coined the term “machine learning” in 1959.

  • 1957

    The Perceptron

    Rosenblatt's learnable weights — a machine that adjusts itself from data.

  • 1986

    Backpropagation

    Popularised for neural networks by Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams. Week 12

  • 1995

    Support Vector Machines

    Cortes & Vapnik. Margins and kernels dominate the next decade. Week 9

  • 2012

    AlexNet

    The ImageNet breakthrough. Deep learning goes from curiosity to default.

  • 2017

    Transformers

    “Attention Is All You Need” — the architecture behind every modern LLM.

  • 2020+

    Foundation models

    GPT-scale language models, diffusion image models, multimodal systems. Week 13

Speaker notes

Original slides 14–15 (Samuel's checkers program: random moves → evaluate the move, then adjust the strategy), placed on a proper timeline.

Two precision points. Say “popularised”, not “invented” for backprop — reverse-mode differentiation goes back to Linnainmaa (1970) and Werbos (1974). And note the field's winters: funding and enthusiasm collapsed in the 1970s and again around 1990. Progress was not monotonic.

The genuinely surprising fact for most students: the core learning algorithm is older than their parents.
SCOPE16/50

03

The biggest confusion:
AI vs ML vs DL

  • Three definitions
  • How they nest
  • Where generative AI sits

Speaker notes

Original slide 16. Ask first: “Are these three words the same thing?” You'll get a split room, which is exactly the point — the confusion is real and worth ten minutes.
SCOPE17/50

Three terms, three scopes

AI

Artificial Intelligence

Any technique that lets a machine mimic, develop or demonstrate human cognition or behaviour.

Includes search, logic, planning and constraint solving — no learning required.

ML

Machine Learning

The science of getting computers to learn from data without being explicitly programmed.

A subset of AI. This course.

DL

Deep Learning

Machine learning using multi-layer neural networks that learn their own representations from raw data.

A subset of ML. CS 4085.

Every deep learning system is machine learning. Every machine learning system is AI. The reverse is not true.

Speaker notes

Original slides 17–19, consolidated onto one comparison.

The clean counter-example that settles it: a chess engine using minimax with alpha-beta pruning is AI and contains no learning at all. Someone wrote every rule. If your students took CS 3081, they built one.

On the DL definition, be precise: depth means learning layered representations. “Learns from raw data” is a consequence, not the definition.
SCOPE18/50

How they nest

Generative AI is the newest ring inside deep learning — applied to producing content rather than only labelling it. It is not a fourth field.New

Speaker notes

Original slide 20, with the innermost ring added.

This is the slide students photograph. Give them time.

Say clearly: ChatGPT is not a separate category from machine learning. It is a very large neural network trained by machine learning on a very large corpus. Every concept in this course — training data, loss, generalization, overfitting, evaluation — applies to it directly. That is why this course is a prerequisite for understanding it, not an alternative to it.

Careful with the innermost ring: most generative models are deep learning, but the ring is a teaching simplification, not a theorem.
DEFINE19/50

04

A formal definition

  • Mitchell's E, T, P
  • A worked example
  • Check your understanding

Speaker notes

DEFINE20/50

A program learns from experience E with respect to task T and performance measure P, if its performance on T, measured by P, improves with E.

Tom Mitchell · 1998

Speaker notes

Original slides 22–23 (French duplicate removed).

Samuel's definition is memorable; Mitchell's is usable. The difference matters: Mitchell's version is a checklist. If you cannot name E, T and P for your problem, you do not yet have a machine learning problem — you have a wish.

Tell them this is the vocabulary of the whole semester. Every lab, every assignment, every project proposal will be examined for a clearly stated E, T and P. It appears on the midterm.
DEFINE21/50

Worked example — playing checkers

  • T — the taskPlaying checkers
  • E — the experiencePlaying many thousands of games against itself
  • P — the performance measureThe proportion of games won against a fresh opponent

Samuel's program improved because all three were present. Remove any one and there is nothing to learn from, nothing to learn, or no way to know whether learning happened.

Speaker notes

Original slide 24.

Drive the last sentence home by removing each element in turn: no E and it can only guess; no T and it has no goal; no P and it can improve without anyone being able to tell.

That third case is the one that ruins real projects. Teams ship models nobody can evaluate. Preview it: “Most people can get a model to train. Far fewer can tell you whether it is any good.”
DEFINE22/50

Check your understanding

Think · 60 seconds · Then we vote

Your email program watches which messages you mark as spam, and uses that to filter better. What is the task T?

  • AClassifying emails as spam or not spam
  • BWatching you label emails as spam or not spam
  • CThe number of emails correctly classified
  • DThis is not a machine learning problem

A is the task. B is the experience E. C is the performance measure P.

Press R to reveal the answer

Speaker notes

Original slides 25–26 (French duplicate removed). The answer is hidden until you press R — take a show of hands on each option first, then reveal.

B and C are the productive wrong answers, because they are E and P. Students who pick them have understood the pieces and mixed up the labels — say so out loud, it keeps them engaged rather than embarrassed.

This exact question format recurs on the midterm.
PARADIGMS23/50

05 · 06 · 07

How machines learn

  • Supervised — learning from answers
  • Unsupervised — learning from structure
  • Reinforcement — learning from consequences

Speaker notes

Original slides 27–29. The organising question: what kind of feedback does the learner get? Answers, no answers, or delayed rewards. Everything else follows from that.
PARADIGMS24/50

Three kinds of feedback

05

Supervised

Every training example comes with the correct answer attached.

Predict the label for examples you haven't seen.

06

Unsupervised

No answers at all — only the data.

Find structure that was already there.

07

Reinforcement

No answers, but a reward signal after acting.

Learn a strategy that maximises reward over time.

A fourth setting matters in practice: self-supervised learning, where the data supplies its own labels — predict the next word, or restore a hidden patch of an image. It is how every large language model is trained.New

Speaker notes

The three-way split is the classical one and it's still the right teaching frame.

But add self-supervision honestly, because it is the single most consequential training paradigm today and the original lecture predates its dominance. The trick is elegant: hide part of the input and make the model predict it. No human labels the internet — the text labels itself. That is how you get a model trained on trillions of words.

Formally it's a clever construction of supervised learning, not a fourth kind of feedback. Say that if pressed. Full treatment in Week 13.
PARADIGMS25/50

Three dimensions of ML classification

The same field can be sliced three ways: by learning style, by task, and by depth. A single model sits in all three at once.

Speaker notes

Original slide 28.

Useful because students often conflate the axes — they think "deep learning" is an alternative to "supervised learning". It isn't. A deep network trained on labelled images is supervised (style), doing classification (task), and deep (depth). Three independent descriptions of one model.

Point at "generative modelling" under Task and note it's the axis we return to in section 08.
PARADIGMS26/50

The algorithm landscape

Almost every named algorithm you will meet this semester lives somewhere on this tree. You are not expected to know them yet — this is the map, not the territory.

Speaker notes

Original slide 29. Do not read the leaves aloud — it would take ten minutes and teach nothing.

Instead use it to reassure and orient: point to Linear Regression (Week 2), k-NN (Week 5), SVM (Week 9), K-Means (Week 10), Neural Networks (Week 12). Say: “Five of these boxes are entire weeks of this course. By December this diagram will read like a table of contents.”

Students photograph this one. Let them.
PARADIGMS27/50

05

Supervised learning

  • Learning from labelled data
  • The training loop
  • Regression vs classification

Speaker notes

PARADIGMS28/50

Supervised learning

We are given a dataset in which the correct output is already known, on the assumption that a relationship exists between input and output. The goal is to recover that relationship well enough to predict outputs for inputs we have never seen.

Regression
Predict a continuous quantity — a price, a temperature, a rainfall amount
Classification
Predict a discrete category — spam or not, benign or malignant, which digit

Speaker notes

Original slide 31.

The distinction is the output type, not the difficulty or the algorithm. Students routinely think regression means "linear" — it doesn't.

The clean test: “Does it make sense to be a little bit wrong?” Predicting 302,000 SAR for a 300,000 SAR house is nearly right. Predicting "benign" for a malignant tumour is not nearly right — it's wrong. Continuous vs discrete.

Weeks 2–3 are regression; Week 4 is classification.
PARADIGMS29/50

How training actually works

That loop is the training phase, and it is the same loop for almost every model in this course. Step 3 is where the mathematics lives — that is gradient descent, and it is Week 2.

Speaker notes

Original slides 32–34 (the French training-phase diagram), rebuilt in English as a cycle.

This is the mechanical heart of the lecture. Trace the arrows with your hand as you speak: predict → measure → adjust → and the dashed arrow carries you back to predict. The loop is the idea.

Two things to point at explicitly. The dashed input at the top — the true answer y — is what makes this supervised; take it away and step 2 is impossible. And the dashed return arrow is the part students underestimate: this runs thousands of times, not once.

Walk the worked example along the bottom slowly. 100 m² goes in, the model guesses 250,000, the truth is 300,000, so the gap is 50,000. “That number is the loss. Training is the process of making it smaller.”

Then: “You will implement exactly this loop by hand in Lab 1. Not a library call — the loop.”

Step 3 is where the mathematics lives; that is gradient descent, and it is Week 2. Today they only need the shape.
PARADIGMS30/50

Regression vs classification

The distinction is the output type, not the difficulty. Ask: “does it make sense to be a little bit wrong?” 302,000 SAR for a 300,000 SAR house is nearly right. “Benign” for a malignant tumour is not.

Speaker notes

Original slides 35 and 37.

Use the credit-risk example to plant ethics early, because Week 11 returns to it: “If the historical data encodes who was approved in the past, the model learns to reproduce those decisions — including the unfair ones.” A model is a mirror of its training data. The syllabus lists ethics as a course emphasis; this is where it starts.

Multi-label often surprises students — the classes aren't mutually exclusive.
PARADIGMS31/50

Three types of classification task

Binary — two classes. Multi-class — one label out of many. Multi-label — several labels at once, because the classes are not mutually exclusive.

Speaker notes

Original slide 37.

Multi-label routinely surprises students. Use the picture: the cat image is simultaneously “cat” and “outdoors” and “railing”. Those are not competing answers — they are all true at once.

Quick check: spam filtering is binary; digit recognition is multi-class; tagging a holiday photo is multi-label.
PARADIGMS32/50

Classification or regression?

In pairs · 90 seconds · Decide for both

  • 1You hold a large inventory of identical items and want to predict how many will sell over the next three months.
  • 2You want software to examine each customer account and decide whether it has been compromised.

Problem 1 is regression — a count is a continuous quantity. Problem 2 is classification — compromised or not.

Watch for the trap: a count is a number, so treat it as regression. “Hacked or not” has exactly two outcomes.

Press R to reveal the answer

Speaker notes

Original slide 36. Run it as a pair discussion, not a lecture — 90 seconds is enough.

Expect argument on problem 1, and the argument is legitimate: sales counts are integers, and a purist would call this count regression (Poisson). At this stage, regression is the right answer. If a strong student raises it, praise it and note that models exist specifically for count data.

Problem 2 is unambiguous.
PARADIGMS33/50

06

Unsupervised learning

  • Structure without answers
  • Clustering
  • Where it's used

Speaker notes

PARADIGMS34/50

Unsupervised learning

We approach the problem with little or no idea what the results should look like, deriving structure from data without knowing the effect of the variables.

Unlabelled dataFind structureGroups

There is no feedback on the predictions, because there are no correct answers to compare against. Evaluation is genuinely harder here.

Speaker notes

Original slides 39–42.

Emphasise the honest difficulty: in supervised learning you can compute accuracy; here you often cannot. If a clustering algorithm returns three groups, who says three is right? Or that the groups mean anything? This is a real, open difficulty, not a gap in their understanding — tell them so.

Mention dimensionality reduction (PCA) alongside clustering so they know unsupervised isn't only clustering. Week 10.
PARADIGMS35/50

Unsupervised learning in the wild

Speaker notes

Original slide 43, with anomaly detection added.

Market segmentation is the crispest contrast with supervised learning: “You are not told the segments and then asked to sort people into them. You are asking whether segments exist at all.”

Anomaly detection is worth the extra card because it explains why you'd choose unsupervised deliberately: with novel fraud you have no labelled examples, because the fraud hasn't happened yet.

The patient-subtype example returns in the closing quiz.
PARADIGMS36/50

07

Reinforcement learning

  • Agent and environment
  • Actions, states, rewards
  • Why it's different

Speaker notes

PARADIGMS37/50

Learning from consequences

1

Observe

The agent perceives the current state of the environment.

2

Act

It chooses an action from those available.

3

Receive

The environment changes state and returns a reward — positive or negative.

4

Adapt

The agent updates its policy: which action to choose in which state.

Nobody tells the agent the right move. It discovers a strategy by acting and living with the results — maximising cumulative reward over time, not reward on the next step.

Speaker notes

Original slides 45–46 (the agent/environment diagram).

Two things make RL genuinely different, and both are worth naming:

Delayed reward. A chess move that loses the game may look fine for twenty moves. Credit assignment across a long sequence is the central difficulty.

Exploration vs exploitation. Do you take the reward you know, or try something new that might be better? A restaurant analogy lands well: your reliable favourite, or the new place.

Samuel's checkers program from earlier is essentially this. Modern examples: AlphaGo, robot locomotion, and — importantly — RLHF, which is how ChatGPT was aligned to be helpful. That connects RL directly to the next section.
TODAY38/50

08

What changed:
generative AI & transfer learning

  • Discriminative vs generative
  • Foundation models
  • Transfer learning & fine-tuning
  • What it doesn't change

Speaker notes

This section is new — it is not in the original 2019-era lecture.

Frame it as a promise kept: everything up to here is the field's foundation, and this is what that foundation now supports. Students arrive already using these tools; if the course never names them, students conclude the course is dated. Name them, and place them correctly inside the map they just learned.
TODAY39/50

Two things a model can do

Discriminative
Learns the boundary between classes.

Given an email, is it spam?
Given a photo, which digit?

Answers questions about data.
Generative
Learns the distribution of the data itself.

Write an email. Draw a digit.
Continue this sentence.

Produces new data.

Everything in sections 05–07 was mostly discriminative. Generative models are trained the same way — data, loss, gradients, generalization — but asked a different question: not “which label?” but “what comes next?”

Speaker notes

The key insight to deliver: generative AI is not a new kind of learning. The training loop from the supervised section is exactly the loop that trains GPT — predict, measure error, adjust, repeat. What changed is the task and the scale.

Concretely, a language model is trained by next-token prediction: given the words so far, predict the next one. Do that across a large fraction of the written internet and something surprising emerges — the model has to learn grammar, facts, and reasoning patterns to predict well.

If asked "is that really all?" — yes, plus RLHF for alignment. The simplicity is the remarkable part.
TODAY40/50

Foundation models

1

Pretrain

Train one very large model on a very large, mostly unlabelled corpus using self-supervision.

2

Adapt

Specialize that model to your task with a small amount of your own data.

3

Deploy

Serve one adapted model — or many, all sharing the same base.

A foundation model is a large pretrained model that serves as a starting point for many downstream tasks. GPT, Claude, Llama, Gemini, Stable Diffusion, and image encoders such as CLIP all follow this pattern.

The economics matter: pretraining costs millions of dollars and enormous compute. Adaptation can cost less than a laptop and an afternoon — which is why you can use these models at all.

Speaker notes

The single most important practical shift since the original lecture: you almost never train from scratch any more.

Make the economic point explicit, because it determines what your students can actually build. Pretraining a frontier model is out of reach for a university lab. Adapting one is a homework assignment. That asymmetry is why foundation models democratized the field rather than centralizing it entirely.

Set expectations for the project: “Your project will almost certainly start from a pretrained model. That is not cheating — it is current practice.”
TODAY41/50

Transfer learning

Huge general datasetPretrained modelYour small datasetSpecialized model

Transfer learning reuses what a model learned on one task to do better on a different, related task — the way a radiologist's years of general training transfer to a new imaging modality in weeks rather than decades.

01

Feature extraction

Freeze the pretrained model, train only a small new output layer on your data.

Fastest. Works with very little data.

02

Fine-tuning

Continue training some or all of the pretrained weights on your data, gently.

Stronger, needs more data and care.

03

Prompting

Don't change the weights at all — describe the task, and give a few examples in the input.

Zero-shot and few-shot. No training at all.

Speaker notes

The most practically valuable slide in the lecture for their projects.

Why it works: the early layers of a vision model learn edges and textures, which are useful for every image task. Only the last layers are task-specific. So keep the general part, replace the specific part.

This directly answers the question every student asks: “I only have 200 labelled images — is that enough?” From scratch, no. With transfer learning, often yes.

Note that prompting is genuinely new conceptually — adapting a model's behaviour without changing a single weight had no real analogue in classical ML. Full treatment in Week 13.
TODAY42/50

What has and hasn't changed

QuestionClassical viewWhat's true today
Where do models come from?Train from scratch on your dataStart from a pretrained model, adapt it
How much labelled data?Thousands to millions of examplesOften dozens — or none, with prompting
What does the model output?A label or a numberAlso text, images, audio, code
Who can build one?Teams with data and computeAnyone with an API key and a good question
Does the training loop change?No. Predict, measure error, adjust, repeat — still exactly the same.
Does overfitting go away?No. Bigger models overfit too. Evaluation matters more, not less.
Does bias in data go away?No — it gets amplified and harder to inspect at scale.

Speaker notes

Read the bottom three rows out loud. They are the reason this course still exists in a world with ChatGPT.

Students often arrive believing large models made the fundamentals obsolete. The opposite is true: when a model is a black box you didn't train, on data you can't inspect, your ability to evaluate it critically is the only defence you have.

Say it directly: “Anyone can call an API. Very few people can tell you whether the output should be trusted. This course makes you the second kind of person.”

Ties to the required reading — Biggio & Roli on adversarial ML — and to the syllabus emphasis on ethics.
PRACTICE43/50

09

The machine learning lifecycle

  • The phases of a real project
  • Where the time actually goes

Speaker notes

PRACTICE44/50

The phases of a project

1

Frame

Define the problem. State T, E and P before writing any code.

2

Collect

Gather and label data. Understand where it came from and who is missing from it.

3

Prepare

Clean, handle missing values, encode, scale, engineer features, split train/val/test.

4

Train

Choose a model family, fit it, tune hyperparameters on validation data.

5

Evaluate

Measure on held-out data. Check failure modes and subgroup performance, not just the average.

6

Deploy

Ship it, monitor it, and retrain as the world drifts away from your training data.

Phases 2 and 3 typically consume most of the project. Phase 4 — the part that looks like machine learning — is often a small fraction of the effort.

Speaker notes

Original slide 28's "phases of ML" idea, made concrete and current.

Set expectations honestly now. Students imagine ML is choosing clever algorithms. In practice most of the work is data: finding it, cleaning it, understanding it, discovering it's wrong. The "80% of the time is data preparation" figure is folklore rather than a measured constant, so say "most" rather than quoting a number.

Phase 6 is the one universities skip and industry lives in: models decay because the world changes. A fraud model trained on 2024 patterns degrades on 2026 fraud.

This is the structure of their semester project. Point that out.

Quiz — E, T and P

Show of hands · No talking yet

We feed a learning algorithm a large amount of historical weather data and have it learn to predict weather. What is a reasonable choice for P?

  • AThe probability of correctly predicting a future date's weather
  • BThe process of examining a large amount of historical weather data
  • CThe weather prediction task itself
  • DNone of these

A. B describes E, and C describes T.

Press R to reveal the answer

Speaker notes

Original slide 48.

Same structure as the earlier spam question, deliberately — repetition of the E/T/P frame is the point. The distractors are again E and T.

Fast: 60 seconds including the vote.

Quiz — which paradigm?

In pairs · 3 minutes · Classify all five

  • 1Predict how many millimetres of rain will fall tomorrow.
  • 2Predict whether a company will win a patent infringement lawsuit.
  • 3Classify a web page as child-friendly or adult.
  • 4Given 50 years of crop yields, predict next year's yield.
  • 5Given records of heart-disease patients, find whether distinct patient groups exist that might need different treatments.

1 regression · 2 classification · 3 classification · 4 regression · 5 unsupervised (clustering)

Press R to reveal the answer

Speaker notes

Original slides 49–52, consolidated into one exercise.

Item 5 is the important one — it's the only unsupervised problem in the set, and after four supervised items in a row students answer on autopilot. The giveaway phrase is "find whether groups exist": nobody is told the groups in advance, so there are no labels to learn from.

If time is short, run items 1 and 5 only. Those two carry the distinction.
NEXT47/50

What to take away

  • The definitionLearning is improving at a task T, measured by P, through experience E
  • Why we need itFor problems whose rules exist but cannot be written down
  • The scopeAI ⊃ ML ⊃ DL ⊃ generative AI — nested, not separate
  • The training loopPredict → measure error → adjust → repeat
  • The paradigmsSupervised, unsupervised, reinforcement — plus self-supervised
  • What's currentFoundation models and transfer learning changed the starting point, not the fundamentals

Speaker notes

Six lines. Read them; don't elaborate. If a student remembers only the second and fourth, the lecture worked.
NEXT48/50

One question to take with you

  • Think of a task you do every week.
  • What would E, T and P be?
  • What data would a model need to learn it?
  • And how would you know it was working?

The last question is the hardest one — and it's the one this course keeps returning to.

Speaker notes

A short reflective close. Nothing to collect — let them sit with it.

Say: “Most people can get a model to train. Far fewer can tell you whether it's actually good. By the end of this semester you will be the second kind.”
